A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OOR research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original pairwise and multi-object evaluations, user studies, scene-editing demonstrations, and a ParaHome-based ablation.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds human-motion synthesis and additional scene-editing demonstrations.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 adds an application-level procedure that optimizes VPoser human poses along generated object trajectories while preserving initial human-object contacts. The core OOR representation, diffusion training objective, and multi-object sampler remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 extends demonstrated task coverage to human motion interacting with two objects, including pouring, cutting, and hanging a hat. Appendix E also adds scene editing on TRUMANS, OAKINK2, and OmniObject3D beyond the retained ParaHome examples.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain SMC and SceneTeller for pairwise generation and GraphDreamer for multi-object generation. The PCA and segmentation ablation variants also remain unchanged; baseline implementation descriptions move to Appendix C.

E3.justification: Retained experiments keep the same scene counts, rendering views, metrics, ControlNet handling, user-study design, and training budget. The revised filtering ratio is a reported outcome, not a changed threshold. The new qualitative applications do not introduce a specified quantitative evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds a qualitative generalization case study testing scene editing across three additional datasets. The existing unseen-mesh and unseen-text analyses remain, while the PCA/segmentation ablation moves from Section 4.4 to Appendix D without substantive changes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed variation, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing score aggregation and statistical estimation practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain all numerical results. v2 adds qualitative motion and cross-dataset editing results, while Figure 6 drops the violin-bow, fork/steak, and hammer/nail examples. Appendix A changes the filtering-ratio range from 0.46–0.88 to 0.58–0.92 without explaining whether this reflects a correction or new measurements.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the human-motion objective in Equation 14, combining a pose-embedding penalty, an angle prior, and contact preservation. Existing OOR mathematics remains substantively unchanged; the Fréchet-distance and instance-scaling formulas are merely relocated and renumbered.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and discussion expand the claimed applications from scene arrangement/editing to human-motion synthesis. The central claims concerning synthetic OOR data, diffusion modeling, and multi-object generation are retained.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly argues that independence from texture and detailed shape makes the synthetic-to-real gap minimal, supported by qualitative editing examples. Section 4.3 also explains how object trajectories can drive human motion through contact preservation. The existing detailed-shape limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the VPoser representation and nearest-vertex contact construction for motion synthesis, although numerical contact counts and loss weights are unspecified. It omits v1's explicit pre-SV3D background-segmentation description; this establishes reduced documentation, not necessarily removal of the implemented step. Existing hardware, training time, and project URL remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds PERSE, DAViD, and the Expressive Body Capture/VPoser reference, including a new connection between DAViD and GenPose-based affordance modeling. Four references supporting the omitted background-segmentation passage disappear. The principal research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations undergo extensive condensation and rewriting. Baseline details move to Appendix C, the main-text ablation becomes Appendix D, and the generality appendix is reorganized into explicit subsections.

P2.justification: v2 adds motion-synthesis Figure 9 and cross-dataset Figure 18, shortens Figure 6 from eight examples to five, and removes a displayed denoising row from Figure 8. The ablation figure and Table 3 move to the appendix, substantially rearranging the experimental presentation.

improvement.justification: The motion-synthesis procedure and demonstrations, together with additional scene-editing datasets, modestly strengthen the paper's practical breadth while preserving its quantitative comparisons and ablation. The gains are limited by qualitative-only validation of the additions, unspecified motion parameters, and reduced preprocessing documentation. The new claim of a minimal synthetic-to-real gap is stronger than the supplied evidence establishes.
